issues.legal_issue: Payments made for a long-term right to extract stones from quarries are capital expenditure rather than deductible revenue expenditure when the right secures a source of raw material from land.
material_facts: The assessee carried on a business of extracting, dressing and selling flagstones.
Under a twelve-year contract, the assessee obtained the exclusive right to extract stones from quarries in six villages, without a limit on the quantity it could extract.
The stones had to be extracted methodically and skilfully from the quarries before they could be dressed and sold.
The contract required annual payments even if no stones were extracted or could be extracted; part of the total obligation was paid in advance and the balance in monthly instalments.
The assessee also had a contract with the Government for quarry rights, but its terms were not produced; the parties and courts treated it as similar in nature to the principal contract.
The assessee claimed the payments as business expenditure, and the tax authorities treated them as capital expenditure.
issues.conclusion: The payments acquired a long-term right to win stones and a capital asset of enduring benefit; they were capital expenditure and were not deductible as business expenditure. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 12(2)(xv) of the Hyderabad Income-tax Act, corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, expenditure is capital if its object is to acquire an asset or enduring advantage for the business, and revenue if it is incurred to run the business or obtain its stock-in-trade. The object of the expenditure, rather than whether payment is made periodically or in a lump sum, determines its character. The Court applied the principles approved in Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax and the enduring-benefit test in Atherton v. British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd.; it distinguished the raw-material arrangements in Mohanlal Hargovind v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Benarsidas Jagannath, and relied on the distinction between raw material and a right to win material from land reflected in Alianza Co. v. Bell and Stow Bardolph Gravel Co. Ltd. v. Poole.

rule.if: income_tax_deduction_appeal and long_term_quarry_right and exclusive_extraction_right and unrestricted_quantity_right and extraction_requires_winning_material_from_land and fixed_obligation_paid_in_installments and payments_due_even_without_extraction

predicates.income_tax_deduction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning whether expenditure claimed in computing business income is deductible.
predicates.long_term_quarry_right: The business obtained a right to extract material from quarries for a long, fixed term.
predicates.exclusive_extraction_right: The contract gave the business the exclusive right to extract material from the specified quarries.
predicates.unrestricted_quantity_right: The contract did not limit the quantity of material the business could extract.
predicates.extraction_requires_winning_material_fro: The material was part of a quarry and had to be extracted from the land before it could be used or sold.
predicates.fixed_obligation_paid_in_installments: The business undertook a fixed payment obligation for the right, with the total amount divided into instalments.
predicates.payments_due_even_without_extraction: The business had to make the payments even when no material was extracted or available for extraction.

issues.definition: When a business appeal concerns a deduction for instalment payments made for an exclusive, long-term and unrestricted right to win material from quarries, and the payments remain due without extraction, the payments are treated as capital and not deductible as business expenses.
